890.title: The Ramgarhia misl
890.hook: Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, a carpenter's son, whose towers still stand at the Harmandir
890.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Jassa Singh Ramgarhia in Sikh histories, and pilgrims to the Harmandir Sahib can see the Ramgarhia Bunga's towers in the same complex.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ahluwalia misl, Jassa Singh's band. Your line was the leader's misl. Did you thank someone who led you? Today, another Jassa Singh, and a very different band. Day eight hundred ninety.

A carpenter's son rides with the Khalsa. Tradition says his family worked with wood and tools, and that he grew up knowing how a thing is put together, joint by joint. Riding didn't stop him being a builder. He built a fort. And beside the Harmandir in Amritsar, towers linked to his name are still standing. His name was Jassa Singh, the same as yesterday's chief, and people told the two apart by their bands. Today: the Ramgarhia misl.
screen: `A CARPENTER'S SON.` → `A BUILDER WHO RODE.` → `TOWERS BY THE HARMANDIR.`

segments.voice: Here's how a band got its name from a building. The first piece is a mud fort. Tradition says that in the hard years, Sikhs raised a small fort of earth near Amritsar and called it Ram Rauni, after Guru Ram Das, who founded the city. It was a place to stand and hold out when the city was threatened. The second piece is the builder. Tradition says Jassa Singh rebuilt and strengthened that fort, and it was renamed Ramgarh, Ram's fort. The men who held it became the Ramgarhias, the band of Ramgarh, and their leader became Jassa Singh Ramgarhia. So this misl wasn't named for a village or a nickname. It was named for a thing that had been built and built again. The third piece is the towers. Beside the Harmandir stands the Ramgarhia Bunga, tall towers that Sikh tradition links to Jassa Singh and his misl. A bunga is a building near the Harmandir where Sikhs could stay, and in the hard years, keep watch. From the top, you could see who was coming. The towers are still there, in the same complex as the Harmandir. And the fourth piece is the name that stayed. Ramgarhia came to be used for Sikhs of carpenter and craftsman families more widely, some of whom were proud to share Jassa Singh's name. A craftsman's son led riders, and the craftsmen kept his name. It's the builder's misl.

segments.voice: Two minutes with something well built. Settle, and look around you. Find one made thing: a chair, a door frame, a mug, the stitching on your sleeve. Let your eyes rest on it. Notice how it's joined. Notice where someone took care: an edge sanded smooth, a seam that holds. Someone's hands did that. On each breath, stay with one detail of it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Ramgarh, Ram's fort at Amritsar, rebuilt and renamed by Jassa Singh, the fort that gave the Ramgarhia misl its name. Today's word.
Your line: the builder's misl. Today, fix or finish one small thing properly, the way a carpenter would. Day eight hundred ninety.

891.title: The Kanhaiya misl
891.hook: Jai Singh Kanhaiya's misl, where Rani Sada Kaur would rise
891.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Rani Sada Kaur in Sikh histories and talks about Sikh women leaders, alongside the Kanhaiya misl founded by Jai Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ramgarhia misl, named for Ramgarh, the fort its carpenter's son rebuilt. Your line was the builder's misl. What did you finish properly? Today, a band that a woman came to lead. Day eight hundred ninety-one.

A son falls in battle. His father, the chief, is old. The band could pass to some cousin, or break apart. Instead, in this story, the young man's widow steps forward. Tradition says she took up the running of the band herself: its lands, its riders, its alliances. Sikh histories remember her as Rani Sada Kaur, and the band she held was one her father-in-law had built. Today: the Kanhaiya misl.
screen: `A SON FALLS IN BATTLE.` → `HIS WIDOW STEPS FORWARD.` → `RANI SADA KAUR.`

segments.voice: Three pieces today. The first is the founder. Jai Singh's band took its name, tradition says, from his home village of Kahna, near Lahore. He became one of the strong chiefs of the misl years, holding land in the hill country and the plains north of Amritsar. The second piece is the loss. Tradition says his son Gurbakhsh Singh was killed in a fight between the misls. That's worth pausing on. The bands that had stood together through the hard century were now, at times, fighting each other. A band of equals can fall out like anyone else. And Jai Singh's heir was gone. The third piece is Sada Kaur. She had married into the family, and with her husband dead, tradition says she became the real power in the misl. She commanded riders. She dealt with other chiefs as an equal. She arranged for her daughter to marry the young heir of another misl, and in the way Sikh histories tell it, she helped that young man rise, with her riders and her counsel. A few days ago on this path, women kept the homes while the riders were away. Here a woman sat with the chiefs, and the young man she helped would one day rule from Lahore, a story for another day. Sada Kaur's band carried her father-in-law's name. But for a time, it was her misl.

Let the scene come back. Notice the moment she decided. On each breath, give that decision its due. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sada Kaur, who came to lead the Kanhaiya misl, Jai Singh's band from Kahna, after her husband fell. Today's word.

892.title: The Sukerchakia misl
892.hook: Charat Singh and Maha Singh's misl, home of the future Maharaja
892.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Sukerchakia misl in Sikh histories as the band of Charat Singh and Maha Singh, from which Maharaja Ranjit Singh came.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kanhaiya misl, and Rani Sada Kaur, who came to lead it. Your line was her misl. Whose lead did you name out loud? Today, the band her daughter married into. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

Sukarchak was a village. Not a city, not a fort, not a place with a famous shrine. Tradition places it in the plains north of Lahore, near Gujranwala. A Sikh named Charat Singh came from there, and the band that gathered round him took the village's name. In the way Sikh histories tell it, it wasn't one of the big misls. Nobody watching those riders would have guessed what their chief's grandson would become. Today: the Sukerchakia misl.
screen: `A VILLAGE CALLED SUKARCHAK.` → `CHARAT SINGH'S BAND.` → `NOT ONE OF THE BIG MISLS.`

segments.voice: Three generations, one at a time. The first is Charat Singh. Tradition says he was a bold, restless chief who built up his band from a small start, raised a fort at Gujranwala, and fought alongside the other misls in the Dal Khalsa. He made the Sukerchakias a band other chiefs had to count. The second is his son, Maha Singh. Tradition says he took up the band young, after his father's death, and carried it further: more villages, more riders, more alliances. It was Maha Singh's son who was promised in marriage to Sada Kaur's daughter, the alliance you heard about yesterday. A small misl was now tied to a strong one. The third generation is a boy named Ranjit Singh. He'll have his own days on this path, so not much about him today, except this: the Maharaja of the Punjab, who would one day rule from Lahore, came out of the Sukerchakia band. Here's what makes that worth a day. Nothing about the beginning looked like a kingdom. A village name. A chief with a fort. A son who kept going. And the riders didn't know the ending. Tradition says neither Charat Singh nor Maha Singh lived to see the boy rule from Lahore. Each did the next thing with the band he had, and the next generation started a little further on. A beginning's size doesn't settle where it goes. The Sukerchakias show what small beginnings look like from the inside.
screen: `CHARAT SINGH BUILDS THE BAND.` · `MAHA SINGH CARRIES IT FURTHER.` · `A BOY CALLED RANJIT SINGH.` · `EACH DID THE NEXT THING.` · then, large: `SMALL BEGINNINGS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with something small. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing in your life that started tiny: a friendship that began with a single conversation, a habit, a plant, a savings jar, a skill you once fumbled. Let yourself remember the very first day of it. How small it was. Then notice where it is now. On each breath, stay with that first small step. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sukarchak, the village Charat Singh came from, which gave the Sukerchakia misl its name; carried further by Maha Singh, it's the band from which the future Maharaja came. Today's word.
Your line: small beginnings. Today, start one thing so small it feels almost silly, and don't judge it by its size. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

893.title: The Nakai misl
893.hook: a misl of the Nakka country south-west of Lahore
893.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Nakai misl in Sikh histories as the band of the Nakka country, and the Nakai name is remembered through the marriage that tied it to Maharaja Ranjit Singh's family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sukerchakia misl, the village of Sukarchak's band that gave the Punjab its future Maharaja. Your line was small beginnings. What small thing did you start? Today, a band named for a whole stretch of country. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

Run back over the names so far. Bhangi: a nickname. Ahluwalia, Kanhaiya, Sukerchakia: villages. Ramgarhia: a fort. Most of those names are a small map of where a band came from. Today's band went wider. Its name doesn't point at one man or one village. It points at a whole stretch of country, south-west of Lahore, that people called the Nakka. The riders were the people of that land. Today: the Nakai misl.
screen: `A NICKNAME, VILLAGES, A FORT.` → `NOW, A WHOLE COUNTRY.` → `THE NAKKA, SOUTH-WEST OF LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Three things about a band named for its land. The first is the land itself. Tradition places the Nakka country south-west of Lahore, in the stretch between the rivers. It was farming country. The Nakai riders came from its villages and held them. They weren't strangers who rode in and took a district. They were its own people, organized as a band of the Khalsa. The second thing is the founder. Tradition says the band grew around a Sikh named Hira Singh, who took amrit, joined the Khalsa, and gathered riders from his country. In the way Sikh histories tell it, the Nakai band wasn't among the largest, and it didn't make the loudest noise in the Dal Khalsa. It held its own corner. The third thing is where the Nakai name turns up later. A daughter of the Nakai family married the young Ranjit Singh, whose band you met yesterday. Tradition says she became the mother of his heir. So the quiet band of the Nakka country ended up woven into the family that ruled from Lahore. Bands that began in different corners of the Punjab were being tied together, by marriage as much as by riding. And here's the thread under all of it. A misl's name kept its origin in plain sight. Say Nakai, and people in the Punjab would know which fields and villages you meant. The band carried its home in its name. It was named for the land.
screen: `THE NAKKA COUNTRY, BETWEEN THE RIVERS.` · `HIRA SINGH GATHERS HIS RIDERS.` · `A NAKAI DAUGHTER MARRIES RANJIT SINGH.` · `A BAND THAT CARRIED ITS HOME IN ITS NAME.` · then, large: `NAMED FOR THE LAND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a place-name. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the name of a place that matters to you: the town you grew up in, your street, the neighborhood your family came from. Say it silently. Do you know what it means, or who it was named for? If you don't, just notice that, and wonder. If you do, let the meaning sit with you. On each breath, hold the place in mind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nakka, the stretch of country south-west of Lahore that gave the Nakai misl its name, gathered by Hira Singh, later tied by marriage to the house of Ranjit Singh. Today's word.
Your line: named for the land. Today, look up what one place-name near you means, and tell someone. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

894.title: The Dallewalia misl
894.hook: a misl north of the Sutlej
894.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Dallewalia misl in Sikh histories, and remember the river Bein at Sultanpur Lodhi, where Gurdwara Ber Sahib marks Guru Nanak's time in its water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nakai misl, the band of the Nakka country. Your line was named for the land. What place-name did you look up? Today, a band that lived along a river. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

On a map of the Punjab, the rivers run down from the mountains like fingers spread across the plain. Between them lie the strips of land people call doabs, the country between two rivers. The bands of riders lived with those rivers: where to cross, when the water was high, which bank you held. Today's band held country along the Sutlej, on its north side. Its name came from a village, but its life came from the water. Today: the Dallewalia misl.
screen: `RIVERS SPREAD ACROSS THE PLAIN.` → `THE LAND BETWEEN TWO RIVERS.` → `A BAND ON THE SUTLEJ.`

segments.voice: Three pieces for a river band. The first is the name. Tradition says the band began with a Sikh from a village called Dallewal, and the riders who joined him were called after it, the Dallewalias. You know the pattern by now: a village, a chief, a band. The second piece is the chief people remembered. Tradition says the band's best-known leader was Tara Singh, called Ghaiba, a hard-riding chief who built up its lands along the Sutlej. In the way Sikh histories tell it, he was a fighter who held his own among bigger misls, and the band's strength rose and fell with him. The third piece is the river itself. For a misl north of the Sutlej, the river was a road, a border and a lifeline at once. It watered the fields that fed the riders. It slowed an army coming from the other bank. It marked where one band's country ended and another's began. To hold land by a river meant knowing it well: the fords, the flood season, the banks that shift. And rivers in this country carry Sikh memory too. North of the Sutlej, at Sultanpur, runs the little river Bein. Tradition says Guru Nanak went into its water one morning and did not come out for days, and came back with the words: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Long before any misl rode, tradition sets a turning point of the Sikh story at a river in the same country. The Dallewalias lived their lives by the river.
screen: `A BAND NAMED FOR DALLEWAL.` · `TARA SINGH GHAIBA, ITS FIGHTER.` · `THE SUTLEJ: ROAD, BORDER, LIFELINE.` · `THE BEIN, WHERE GURU NANAK WENT IN.` · then, large: `BY THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a river. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the nearest river to where you live, or one you've known: its color, its sound, the bridge you cross it on. If you don't know its name, that's worth noticing. Picture where it comes from and where it goes. On each breath out, let it keep flowing in your mind. If you can, later, look at a map and trace it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Dallewal, the village that gave the Dallewalia misl its name, built up by Tara Singh Ghaiba, holding land along the north side of the Sutlej. Today's word.
Your line: by the river. Today, find out where your water comes from: which river, which lake, which well. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

895.title: The Nishanwalia misl
895.hook: the standard-bearers of the Dal Khalsa
895.howItsDone: Sikhs raise the Nishan Sahib outside gurdwaras and change its cloth with care at set times, and the Nishanwalia misl is remembered in Sikh histories as the Dal Khalsa's standard-bearers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dallewalia misl, named for the village of Dallewal, a band that lived along the Sutlej. Your line was by the river. Did you find where your water comes from? Today, a band named for what it carried. Day eight hundred ninety-five.

Dust, noise, horses everywhere, and no radio, no phone, no way to shout loud enough. In a battle like that, how do so many riders know where their own side is? They look for the flag. Whoever holds it up tells everyone else: we're still here, gather to this. Tradition says one band of the Khalsa had that job in the Dal Khalsa, and got its name from it. Today: the Nishanwalia misl.
screen: `DUST, NOISE, NO WAY TO SHOUT.` → `LOOK FOR THE FLAG.` → `ONE BAND HAD THAT JOB.`

segments.voice: Three pieces today. The first is the word. Nishan means a flag, a standard, a mark. Nishanwalia means the ones of the flag. This band wasn't named for a village or a fort. It was named for a duty. The second piece is the duty itself. Tradition says that when the Dal Khalsa rode together, this band carried the Khalsa's standard, and its first chief, Dasaundha Singh, was its bearer. Carrying the flag wasn't a ceremony. The bearer rode where the fighting was, because the flag had to be seen. If it went down, riders lost their way. So the bearer was guarded, and he guarded something bigger than his band: the sign that the Khalsa was still standing. In the way Sikh histories tell it, the Nishanwalias were not a large misl. Their honor came from what they carried for everyone else. The third piece is the flag you can still see. Outside gurdwaras flies the Nishan Sahib, a tall pole wrapped in cloth, with a saffron or deep blue flag bearing the Khalsa's emblem. Sikhs say it marks a place where anyone can come in, eat in the langar and find shelter. Tradition traces the custom back to the Gurus' own time. The Nishanwalias carried one in battle. Sikh communities raise one over their gurdwaras. Either way, the flag says the same thing: we're here, and you can find us. The band was the flag-bearers.

If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nishan, a flag or standard, the duty that named the Nishanwalia misl, who carried the Dal Khalsa's standard so every rider could see where to gather. Today's word.

896.title: The Singhpuria misl
896.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Nawab Kapur Singh in Sikh histories and gurdwara talks as a leader known for seva, and the Singhpuria misl as the band that came from his village.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nishanwalia misl, named for the Nishan, the band that carried the Dal Khalsa's standard. Your line was the flag-bearers. What did you carry for someone? Today, the band of a man who carried a fan. Day eight hundred ninety-six.

The man with the fan. Earlier on this path you met him at Amritsar, moving the air over the sangat on a hot day, when the title of nawab found him. Nawab Kapur Singh went on to lead the Khalsa through the hard years. But the title came to a man who already had home ground. He had his own village, and his own riders, and they had a name. Today, not the title and not the fan. Today: the Singhpuria misl.
screen: `THE MAN WITH THE FAN.` → `A LEADER OF EVERYONE.` → `AND HIS OWN RIDERS.`

segments.voice: Three pieces. The first is a renamed village. Tradition says Kapur Singh took a village called Faizullapur, near Amritsar, and renamed it Singhpura, the town of the Singhs. His band took the new name: the Singhpurias. Some histories still call them by the old name too, the Faizullapurias. So the misl's name holds a small act of claiming: a village renamed for the Khalsa. The second piece is the size of the band. In the way Sikh histories tell it, the Singhpuria misl was not among the great misls in riders or land. And that's the surprise. The man who held the title of nawab, the man the chiefs followed through the hard century, led a modest band of his own. He could have used his place at the head of the Khalsa to make his own riders the strongest. Tradition doesn't remember him doing that. The third piece is who came after him. When Kapur Singh grew old, tradition says, the leadership of the whole Khalsa did not pass to his own band. It went to Jassa Singh, from the Ahluwalias, the rider he had trained. His own misl carried on under its own chiefs, and the leadership of everyone went where he judged it should go. That's an unusual kind of leader. A nawab whose band stayed modest. A chief who handed the biggest job outside his own circle. Sikh histories dwell on his humility: the fan, the stables, the robe touched to the feet of five Sikhs. The Singhpuria misl is the same humility, written in the map. It's the nawab's band.
screen: `FAIZULLAPUR RENAMED SINGHPURA.` · `A MODEST BAND FOR A NAWAB.` · `THE LEADERSHIP PASSED OUTSIDE IT.` · `HUMILITY WRITTEN IN THE MAP.` · then, large: `THE NAWAB'S BAND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with something you passed on. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time you could have kept something for yourself and handed it to someone else instead: a seat, a role, the last slice, a job you let a newer person try. Or a time you held on. Don't judge either. Let the moment come back: what it cost you, and what it gave them. On each breath, let it sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
